questions.q: At which OSI layer do routers make forwarding decisions based on IP addresses?
questions.explain: Routers work at Layer 3 (Network), forwarding packets by destination IP address. Switches work at Layer 2 using MAC addresses.

questions.q: A traditional switch forwards frames using MAC addresses. Which OSI layer is that?
questions.explain: MAC addresses and frames belong to Layer 2 (Data Link). Layer 3 switches can also route, but classic switching is Layer 2.

questions.q: What is the PDU (protocol data unit) called at the Transport layer when using TCP?
questions.explain: Transport = segment (a UDP PDU is often called a datagram), Network = packet, Data Link = frame, Physical = bits.

questions.q: What is the PDU called at the Data Link layer?
questions.explain: Layer 2 wraps the packet in a header (MACs) and trailer (FCS) to create a frame.

questions.q: Which transport protocol is connection-oriented and uses a three-way handshake?
questions.explain: TCP sets up a connection (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), numbers its segments, acknowledges them and retransmits lost data. UDP does none of that.

questions.q: Put the TCP three-way handshake in order.
questions.explain: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK. After the ACK, the connection is ESTABLISHED and data can flow.

questions.q: Why do real-time voice and video usually use UDP instead of TCP?
choices: Low overhead: a late retransmitted packet is useless anyway
questions.explain: For live audio/video, waiting for a retransmission adds delay. UDP's low overhead and lack of retransmission suit real-time traffic.

questions.q: How long is an Ethernet MAC address?
questions.explain: MAC addresses are 48 bits, written as 12 hex digits such as 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. 32 bits is IPv4; 128 bits is IPv6.

questions.q: What do the first 24 bits of a MAC address identify?
questions.explain: The first 3 bytes are the Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI) assigned by the IEEE to the vendor. The last 3 bytes are vendor-assigned.

questions.q: Which is the Ethernet broadcast MAC address?
questions.explain: All 48 bits set to 1 (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF) is the broadcast address. Every device in the broadcast domain processes it.

questions.q: Which device separates broadcast domains by default?
questions.explain: Routers do not forward broadcasts, so each router interface is a separate broadcast domain. Switches forward broadcasts out all ports in the VLAN.

questions.q: On which device is EACH port its own collision domain, while all ports share one broadcast domain?
questions.explain: A switch gives each port a separate collision domain, but by default all ports (in one VLAN) are in the same broadcast domain. A hub is one big collision domain.

questions.q: Without Auto-MDIX, which cable type connects a PC to a switch?
questions.explain: Unlike devices (PC↔switch, router↔switch) use straight-through. Like devices (switch↔switch, PC↔PC) traditionally need crossover. Auto-MDIX on modern gear fixes either.

questions.q: Without Auto-MDIX, which cable type connects two switches together?
questions.explain: Switch to switch is 'like to like', so a crossover cable swaps the transmit and receive pairs.

questions.q: What is the maximum standard segment length for twisted-pair Ethernet (Cat5e/Cat6)?
questions.explain: Copper twisted-pair Ethernet (10BASE-T through 1000BASE-T) is limited to 100 m. Use fiber for longer runs.

questions.q: Which fiber type is best for very long distances (many kilometers)?
questions.explain: Single-mode fiber has a tiny core and usually a laser light source, reaching tens of km. Multimode (LED/VCSEL, larger core) is cheaper but shorter range.

questions.q: The TCP/IP model's Application layer maps to which OSI layers?
questions.explain: TCP/IP folds Session (5), Presentation (6) and Application (7) into a single Application layer.

questions.q: Order the encapsulation process as data travels DOWN the stack on the sending host.
questions.explain: Application data gets a Transport header (segment), then an IP header (packet), then a Layer 2 header and trailer (frame), and finally goes out as bits.

questions.q: Order the OSI layers from Layer 1 to Layer 7.
questions.explain: Bottom up: 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away'. Top down: 'All People Seem To Need Data Processing'.

questions.q: What does ARP do?
choices: Resolves a known IPv4 address to a MAC address
Resolves a hostname to an IP address
Finds the best route to a network
questions.explain: ARP broadcasts 'Who has 10.0.0.1?' and the owner replies with its MAC. DNS resolves names; DHCP assigns addresses; routing protocols find routes.

questions.q: Which protocol do ping and traceroute rely on?
questions.explain: ping sends ICMP Echo Requests and waits for Echo Replies. traceroute uses rising TTLs and listens for ICMP Time Exceeded messages.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the TTL field in an IPv4 header?
choices: Stop packets looping forever: each router decrements it and drops the packet at 0
Set how long a DNS record is cached
questions.explain: Every router decrements TTL by 1 and discards the packet when it reaches 0, sending an ICMP Time Exceeded back. traceroute exploits exactly this.

questions.q: Which TCP flag signals a graceful end to a connection?
questions.explain: FIN says 'I have no more data to send'. Each side sends FIN and ACKs the other's. RST aborts a connection abruptly.

questions.q: One end of a link is full duplex and the other is half duplex. What symptom is most typical?
choices: Late collisions and CRC errors, with slow throughput
The link will not come up at all
questions.explain: A duplex mismatch keeps the link up but performs terribly. The half-duplex side sees late collisions; the full-duplex side sees CRC/runt errors.

questions.q: What is the default Ethernet MTU in bytes?
questions.explain: Standard Ethernet MTU is 1500 bytes of payload. 'Jumbo frames' (often 9000 bytes) must be enabled on every device in the path.

questions.q: Every device connects to one central switch. What topology is that?
questions.explain: A star topology uses a central device. It's the most common LAN design; the switch is a single point of failure unless made redundant.

questions.q: Which IEEE standard family defines Ethernet?
questions.explain: 802.3 = Ethernet. 802.11 = Wi-Fi, 802.1Q = VLAN tagging, 802.15 = Bluetooth/PAN.

questions.q: Which TCP mechanism lets a receiver limit how much unacknowledged data the sender can transmit?
questions.explain: The TCP window size advertises how many bytes the receiver can accept. A sliding window provides flow control.

questions.q: What is the range of 'well-known' port numbers?
questions.explain: Well-known: 0–1023. Registered: 1024–49151. Dynamic/ephemeral (client source ports): 49152–65535.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a characteristic of UDP?
questions.explain: UDP is connectionless and fire-and-forget with an 8-byte header. Reliability (ACKs, retransmission) belongs to TCP.

questions.q: Sending one packet to a GROUP of interested receivers is called:
questions.explain: Unicast = one-to-one, broadcast = one-to-all (in the subnet), multicast = one-to-group (subscribers), anycast = one-to-nearest.

questions.q: Which OSI layer handles data formatting, encryption and compression?
questions.explain: Presentation (6) translates data formats (ASCII, JPEG) and can encrypt or compress. Session (5) manages dialogs between applications.

questions.q: An interface shows rising CRC errors. What is the most likely cause?
choices: A Layer 1 problem: a bad cable, connector or interference
questions.explain: CRC errors mean frames arrived corrupted, which usually points to cabling, bad optics, EMI or a duplex mismatch. Start at Layer 1!

questions.q: A switch receives a frame whose destination MAC is NOT in its MAC address table. What does it do?
choices: Floods it out all ports in the VLAN except the one it came in on
Sends it back to the sender
Sends an ARP request for the MAC
questions.explain: Unknown unicast frames are flooded. When the destination replies, the switch learns its MAC from the reply's source address.

questions.q: How does a switch build its MAC address table?
choices: It reads the SOURCE MAC of each incoming frame
It reads the DESTINATION MAC of each frame
An administrator must type every entry
questions.explain: Switches learn by recording source MAC + incoming port. Entries age out (default 300 seconds on Cisco) if not refreshed.

questions.q: What is a host's default gateway?
choices: The router interface the host uses to reach other networks
The switch the host is plugged into
questions.explain: Traffic destined outside the local subnet is sent to the default gateway, usually a router (or Layer 3 switch) interface in the same subnet.

questions.q: Which of these protocols runs over UDP?
questions.explain: TFTP uses UDP 69. SSH (22), HTTP (80) and SMTP (25) use TCP. Other UDP favorites: DNS queries, DHCP, SNMP, Syslog, NTP.

questions.q: Order these network types from SMALLEST to LARGEST geographic scope.
questions.explain: PAN (Bluetooth around you) < LAN (a building) < MAN (a city) < WAN (countries; the internet is the largest WAN).

questions.q: What layer NUMBER is the Transport layer in the OSI model?
questions.explain: Transport is Layer 4 (TCP/UDP, ports, segments).

questions.q: In the IPv4 header's Protocol field, what number identifies TCP?
questions.explain: Protocol 6 = TCP, 17 = UDP, 1 = ICMP, 89 = OSPF. The Protocol field tells the receiver which upper-layer protocol gets the payload.

questions.q: In the IPv4 header's Protocol field, what number identifies UDP?
questions.explain: UDP = 17, TCP = 6, ICMP = 1.

questions.q: Test reachability to Google's public DNS server at 8.8.8.8.
questions.hint: The classic ICMP echo command, followed by the IP.
questions.output:
PING 8.8.8.8 (8.8.8.8) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 8.8.8.8: icmp_seq=1 ttl=117 time=11.4 ms
64 bytes from 8.8.8.8: icmp_seq=2 ttl=117 time=11.1 ms
--- 8.8.8.8 ping statistics ---
2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss
questions.explain: `ping` sends ICMP Echo Requests. Replies prove Layer 3 reachability in both directions. On Linux add `-c 4` to stop after 4 pings.

questions.q: Show every router hop between you and 1.1.1.1.
questions.hint: Linux uses traceroute; Windows uses tracert.
questions.explain: traceroute sends probes with TTL 1, 2, 3... Each router that drops a probe (TTL hit 0) replies with ICMP Time Exceeded, revealing the path. Windows calls it `tracert`.

questions.q: Display your machine's ARP cache (IP-to-MAC mappings).
questions.hint: Modern Linux: `ip neigh`. Old school (and Windows): `arp -a`.
questions.output:
192.168.1.1 dev wlan0 lladdr 3c:84:6a:12:9f:01 REACHABLE
192.168.1.23 dev wlan0 lladdr a4:5e:60:c1:22:7b STALE
questions.explain: `ip neigh` (or `arp -a`) shows learned neighbors. If your gateway's entry is missing or INCOMPLETE, you have a Layer 2 problem.

questions.q: Which three-letter protocol maps a known IPv4 address to a MAC address?
questions.explain: ARP, the Address Resolution Protocol. In IPv6 that job moves to NDP (Neighbor Discovery, part of ICMPv6).

questions.q: Which connector and cable do you use to reach a Cisco device's CLI with no network configured?
choices: A console (rollover) cable to the console port
A crossover cable to any Ethernet port
A straight-through cable to the AUX port with Telnet
questions.explain: Out-of-box access is through the console port using a rollover/console cable (or USB console) and a terminal emulator at 9600 baud.

questions.q: What kind of cable does 1000BASE-T use?
questions.explain: The 'T' means twisted pair. 1000BASE-SX/LX are fiber variants. 1000BASE-T uses all four pairs of Cat5e or better.
